# A Note on AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning title="Working draft: Unverified text"}
**This text is an active, evolving work in progress.** This book will ultimately undergo the exact same rigorous, line-by-line human expert review that grounded earlier foundational texts in this curriculum, but it has not reached that stage yet. It is shared openly as an early draft to invite community critique and collective refinement.
:::

This book is released as an open-access, living textbook; it is not yet under contract with a commercial publisher. In earlier works, computing systems and software infrastructure was my native intellectual home. But *Physical AI* pushes across the causal boundary into unfamiliar terrain: classical kinematics, control barrier functions, actuator thermodynamics, and hard real-time latency budgets.

The foundational challenge of this project began with collecting ideas, organizing disparate concepts, and shaping the curriculum: deciding which physical dynamics require a chapter, what belongs in a section, and what to omit so that students can digest the material from first principles.

In conducting this cross-disciplinary survey across robotics, control theory, and machine learning infrastructure, I leveraged generative AI as an interactive search tool and synthesis partner. Much like using an advanced search engine to explore unfamiliar domains and assemble notes on a blank page, large language models helped surface relevant papers, identify historical precedents, and connect dots between classical control literature and modern learned systems that even an experienced systems researcher might not initially spot. Navigating that cross-disciplinary boundary was intellectually demanding, yet deeply rewarding in revealing how classical Newtonian mechanics and statistical learning intersect.

A textbook is fundamentally an architectural distillation; the primary credit belongs to the researchers, roboticists, and control theorists whose discoveries populate our bibliography. At the same time, an AI search tool can only propose candidate papers and surface connections; it cannot make the physical engineering calls. Deciding which physical constraints belong in this curriculum, ensuring that mathematical analogies respect real-time latency budgets, actuator limits, and functional safety, and determining what to omit so that students can reason from first principles required months of demanding labor, late nights, and iterative rewriting.

Authorship in this domain is stewardship: uniting two historically siloed worlds and assuming responsibility for the resulting engineering framework. My name is on the cover so that readers have a single human being to hold accountable—someone to reach out to for clarifications, debates, and corrections.

In the physical world, errors carry kinetic consequences: delay is paid in millimeters, and unhandled failure results in mechanical damage or physical harm. For that very reason, **this unverified draft must be read with rigorous skepticism**. While our executable Python cells verify numerical consistency and continuous integration tests check reference hygiene, the systems architectures presented here have not yet completed the comprehensive one-on-one human expert review that will precede final publication.

I invite readers, roboticists, and systems engineers to read critically, report errors on GitHub, challenge the proposed models, and help us turn this working draft into a safe and verified foundation for embodied machine learning.

The principle holds with absolute finality at the physical boundary: **the tool can propose, and the tool can tutor, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.**
